title: Node pressure gradient analysis and mitigation playbook (WIP)
content:
Purpose:
This is a working playbook and incident analysis for a run of node pressure events we observed across eu-west-1 on 2025-10-29 through 2025-11-02. The emphasis here is on the notion of a pressure gradient — where nodes on the same ASG show a progressive worsening of memory+io pressure before full eviction waves — and on quick mitigations that preserve low-latency serving while stabilizing the cluster.

High-level summary:
- Symptom: gradual rise in pod start latency and failed scheduling for bursty inference pods, followed by kubelet OOMKills and high pod eviction rates on a subset of edge/gpu nodes.
- Impact: ~8% of customer requests returned 5xx during the peak (short windows), rolling degradations in tail latency for several models. No data loss.
- Detection: custom alert "node_pressure_gradient" fired after we saw 3 nodes in the same ASG exceed soft_eviction_cpu/ memory thresholds within 12 minutes.
- Immediate mitigations applied: scale-out ASG (temporary), cordon high-pressure nodes, throttle image pulls with node-level admission control, applied eviction soft limits tweak to allow short-term burst capacity.

Timeline (approx):
- 2025-10-29 02:12 UTC: first anomalous increase in kube_pod_start_time_p95 on node-gpu-1c.
- 2025-10-29 02:20 UTC: node-gpu-1c pod failures increase; kubelet logs show repeated image pull backoffs + continuations of large KV-cache writes.
- 2025-10-29 02:30 UTC: node-gpu-1b reports elevated containerd image-pull queue length and increasing iowait.
- 2025-10-29 02:40 UTC: alert fires: node_pressure_gradient (ASG eu-west-1-gpu-pool), pager to SRE oncall.
- 02:45–03:15 UTC: actions: cordon node-gpu-1c, trigger ASG scale out + schedule traffic routing away from affected AZ.
- 03:30 UTC: progressive evictions observed on node-gpu-1d despite cordon (evictions triggered by kubelet local threshold replay after resource reclaim).
- 04:00 UTC: cluster begins to stabilize after scaled capacity + local throttles. Post-incident monitoring shows p95 latency back to baseline by 04:30.

Key metrics observed (examples):
- kube_pod_start_time_p95: +420% vs baseline on affected nodes.
- node_memory_available_bytes: falling rapidly on nodes that later failed.
- node_disk_io_time_seconds_total: sustained rise; iowait correlated with containerd/image-pull spikes.
- cni_tx_drop_total and cni_rx_drop_total: small transient spikes when node experienced heavy concurrency.
- containerd_image_pull_queue_length: peaked at ~120 on one node.

Primary hypotheses considered:
1) Large image pulls (concurrent) + limited disk iops created IO starvation for kubelet and container runtime, causing pods to stall in init and memory not getting reclaimed.
2) Underestimation of resident KV cache growth for long-running transformer workloads causing steady memory creep until kernel reclaim became aggressive, triggering pod evictions.
3) CNI queueing + netns buffer exhaustion contributed to tail latency and exacerbated perceived pressure (services timeouts triggered more retries -> more load).
4) Systemd OOMKiller interactions — we observed that some OOMs were kernel-initiated and not kubelet-initiated, leading to partial-state processes.

Diagnostics we ran (commands to reproduce / for runbook):
- node-level inspection:
  - kubectl get nodes -o wide --show-labels | grep eu-west-1-gpu
  - kubectl describe node node-gpu-1c  # look for eviction signals, daemonset events
  - journalctl -u kubelet -n 500 --no-pager | sed -n '1,200p'
  - sudo iostat -xz 1 10  # check iowait and device util
  - sudo /usr/local/bin/containerd-ctr tasks ps | wc -l; containerd metrics endpoint for queue length
- kube observability:
  - prometheus: increase query window and compare node_memory_available_bytes and kubelet_eviction{type=~"memory|imagefs"}
  - grafana dashboard: node exporter per-node iops and disk latency charts
- cni checks:
  - ip -s link show <cni-iface> for rx/tx drops
  - check CNI logs on node for flaps (/var/log/xx-cni.log)

Temporary mitigation steps (blue-team immediate play):
- cordon affected nodes: kubectl cordon node-gpu-1c
- reduce admission for large image pulls: patch admission controller to set imagePullBackoff limit for specific bursty deployers (short-term).
- ASG scale-out: trigger autoscaler emergency policy to add 3 nodes into eu-west-1-gpu-pool (manual trigger if autoscaler lagging).
- lower kubelet eviction thresholds only for soft eviction (give headroom): set kubelet flag --eviction-soft to memory.available<150Mi for 120s for test nodes (note: dangerous; use guarded rollout).
- deploy temporary node-local registry cache to reduce image pulls on hot start spikes.

Why we didn't do some actions during incident:
- We avoided mass rebooting of the node pool because the KV cache persistence across node restarts was uncertain for long-running model processes.
- We did not immediately increase kubelet allocatable memory because doing so on all nodes risked masking an underlying leak.

Post-incident root cause (convergent hypothesis):
- The incident was driven by the combination of large concurrent image pulls (from a bursty deploy pipeline) plus sustained memory growth in model processes that was within per-container limits but grew the node memory pressure over hours. The IO pressure amplified the problem by delaying kubelet progress and image pulls, creating a feedback loop: slower image pulls -> longer init -> more concurrent retries and longer-lived pods -> more KV/cache growth -> memory pressure -> OOM/evictions. CNI contributed minorly via RX/TX drops under extreme egress bursts.

Short-term follow-ups (next 7 days):
- SRE-3421: Create an emergency gate in the CI/CD pipeline to limit concurrent model deploys in a single ASG. (Owner: Jamal)
- SRE-3422: Add per-node containerd image-pull queue length alert (threshold 40 sustained for 3m). (Owner: Sophie)
- SRE-3423: Deploy node-local image cache DaemonSet in eu-west-1 and run a one-week canary. (Owner: Arjun)

Longer-term work (quarter roadmap items):
- Add a new metric "node_pressure_gradient_score" that computes weighted z-score across nodes in an ASG to surface progressive degradation earlier. (Product+SRE)
- Work with runtime team to add KV cache accounting to cgroups so we can attribute memory usage to the model process more accurately (research task).
- Investigate moving large model images to a layered cache strategy and reduce cold-start pulls by pre-warming nodes for scheduled rollouts.
- Revisit kubelet eviction policy defaults for GPU pools; propose a two-tiered eviction approach that prefers disk/imagefs eviction before memory in controlled windows.

Draft runbook (for SREs oncall) — immediate checklist:  (copyable steps)
1) Acknowledge alert -> post short status in #sre-oncall with ASG, affected node list.
2) Run quick primer commands: kubectl get nodes --selector=pool=gpu -o wide; kubectl top nodes | sort -k2 -n 
3) If 2+ nodes in ASG have node_memory_available_bytes dropping by >50% in 10m: cordon the most affected node: kubectl cordon <node> and drain non-critical DaemonSets (kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force).
4) Check containerd image pull queue: query /metrics on containerd or use containerd-ctr; if queue length > 40 sustained -> trigger ASG scale or start node-local cache.
5) Inspect kubelet logs for kernel OOM or eviction manager messages: journalctl -u kubelet -n 200 | grep -E "eviction|oom|image pull"
6) If IO wait > 20% across the node: avoid immediate kubelet flag changes; instead reduce admission (pause CI) and add capacity.
7) Escalation: open SRE incident ticket and loop in runtime eng (label: runtime-oncall) if kernel OOMs detected.
8) Post-stabilization: collect artifacts: tar /var/log/kubelet.log, containerd metrics, cni logs, and snapshot Prometheus queries for the 1h window around the peak.

Monitoring and alerts suggested (draft thresholds):
- containerd_image_pull_queue_length per-node: warn 20 for 3m, critical 40 for 2m.
- node_memory_available_bytes percent drop: warn 30% drop in 10m, critical 50% drop in 5m across 2 nodes in ASG.
- node_disk_io_time_seconds_total: critical if device_utilization > 90% for 2m.
- ASG-pressure-gradient alert: trigger when 3 nodes in a single ASG have memory drop >20% sequentially within 15m.

Dashboards to create/update:
- ASG pressure gradient overview (ASG lanes showing per-node z-score over time).
- Node image-pull queue dashboard (per-node heatmap for containerd queue length).
- Kubelet eviction event timeline with concurrent disk and network metrics.

Open questions / TODOs (notes-to-self):
- How to best cap concurrent deploys from our CI without adding too much friction for model teams? (proposal: sliding window gate per-ASG)
- Should we try a kubelet tuning experiment that prefers imagefs eviction first on GPU nodes? Safety checks needed.
- Confirm whether the OOMs are triggered by user container memory or by kernel slabs/caches; need pmap like tooling to attribute.

Appendix: Useful commands and artifacts to attach to incident ticket:
- kubectl get events --all-namespaces --field-selector reason=Evicted --sort-by=.lastTimestamp -n kube-system
- for node in node-gpu-*; do echo $node; kubectl describe node $node | egrep "Evicted|Pressure"; done
- sudo iotop -b -o -qq 5  # watch top IO consumers
- collectd/prometheus query examples: rate(containerd_image_pull_queue[2m]) and increase(kubelet_runtime_operations_duration_seconds_count[5m])

Postmortem notes template (short):
- Summary, Impact window, Root cause hypothesis, Contributing factors (imagepull + kv cache growth + io), Corrective actions (short-term), Preventive actions (long-term), Owners and deadlines.

Last thoughts:
This felt like a slow-burn failure mode that we can detect earlier if we instrument the runtime queues and treat image-pull backoffs as a first-class indicator of node stress. Putting a cheap node-local cache in front of container registry is probably the fastest ROI. Also need to prevent CI pipelines from creating deployment storms over a shared ASG.

Notes to self: add sketches for the ASG pressure z-score calculation and share with metrics team next week.

-- Leah
